prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "TORONTO DOMINION BANK" (ticker TD), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "TD", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: The Toronto-Dominion Bank
markets: Canadian personal banking (chequing and savings accounts, mortgages, credit cards, auto loans)
US retail and commercial banking on the East Coast (TD Bank, America's Most Convenient Bank)
Wealth management, direct investing and asset management (TD Wealth, TD Direct Investing, TD Asset Management)
Property and casualty and life insurance in Canada (TD Insurance)
Capital markets and investment banking (TD Securities, TD Cowen)

mission.statement: To enrich the lives of our customers, communities and colleagues.
mission.source: TD's stated purpose, published on TD Stories ('Bringing our purpose to life', stories.td.com) and in TD annual reports
mission.plain: TD wants to make life better for the people who bank with it, the towns it works in and the people who work for it.

about.plain: TD is one of Canada's two biggest banks and also runs a large bank along the US East Coast. It keeps people's money safe, lends them money for homes, cars and businesses, and gives out credit cards. It also helps people invest and save for retirement, sells home and car insurance, and helps big companies raise money. It earns money from the gap between what it pays savers and what it charges borrowers, and from fees.
about.customers: Over 17 million people and businesses in Canada and more than 10 million in the US, plus big companies, governments and investors.
about.everyday: Its green TD logo is on bank branches and ATMs across Canada and the US East Coast, and many Canadians insure their car or home with TD Insurance.

money.plain: Bank accounts, mortgages, credit cards and business loans in Canada
Bank accounts, mortgages, cards and business loans at TD Bank in the eastern US
Investing accounts, advice, mutual funds and home, car and life insurance

money.part: Wholesale banking (TD Securities and TD Cowen)
money.plain: Trading, investment banking and loans for big companies and governments

result.summary: TD has a durable competitive advantage in Canada, where it is one of the two largest banks in a tightly regulated five-bank oligopoly with a huge, cheap and sticky deposit base and leading positions in cards, direct investing and insurance. That showed in FY2025 reported revenue of C$67,777M and net income of C$20,538M (30.3% net margin, boosted by a C$8,975M pre-tax gain on selling its Schwab stake) and a reported ROE of 15.8% in Q3 2026. Its US franchise is large but has been weakened by the October 2024 anti-money-laundering guilty plea, US$3.088 billion of penalties and a US$434 billion asset cap on its US bank.

pricingPower.evidence: Canada's concentrated banking market lets TD hold spreads and fees: nine-month FY2026 Canadian Personal and Commercial Banking revenue rose 5.3% to C$16,194M and Q3 2026 reported ROE reached 15.8%, while FY2025 non-interest income rose to C$34,715M from C$26,751M (partly the Schwab gain); but loan and deposit pricing follows Bank of Canada and Fed rates, and its US bank cannot grow its balance sheet past the US$434 billion asset cap.

moats.evidence: TD, with roots back to 1855, is one of the best-known brands in Canada and its green logo and long branch hours ('America's Most Convenient Bank') are well known on the US East Coast, though the 2024 US AML guilty plea dented its reputation.
Customers with mortgages, chequing accounts, credit cards (TD Aeroplan Visa), investments and insurance at TD rarely move, supporting C$645,173M of personal deposits at July 31, 2026.
Its large branch and ATM networks in Canada and the US give convenience, but banking has few true network effects.

With C$2,111,861M of assets at July 31, 2026, TD spreads technology, compliance and marketing costs over one of the largest revenue bases in Canada (28.5% of the Big Five's combined FY2025 revenue), and is targeting C$2-2.5B of annualized cost savings under its 2025 Investor Day plan.
Canada's market is dominated by five big banks under strict OSFI regulation, leaving little room for new entrants to reach scale.
TD is an incumbent being challenged by low-fee digital players such as Wealthsimple, EQ Bank and Tangerine rather than the reverse.

TD's retail service model was a strength, but the US AML failures that led to the October 2024 guilty plea exposed serious weaknesses in risk and control processes that it is still remediating (about US$550M of remediation spend expected in FY2026).
Its banking licences and low-cost deposit base (C$1,260,724M of deposits at July 31, 2026) are valuable but shared with the other big banks rather than exclusive.

customers.evidence: TD serves about 17 million clients in Canada and more than 10 million in the US and keeps them through bundled products, but in J.D. Power's 2025 Canada Retail Banking Satisfaction Study RBC ranked highest among the Big Five and Tangerine among midsize banks, and the US AML scandal hurt trust.

talent.evidence: With more than 100,000 colleagues TD is one of Canada's largest employers and a major graduate recruiter, but it has been cutting management layers (from 10 to 8) and over 3% of non-client-facing roles under its restructuring, and lost senior leaders in the AML fallout.

product.evidence: TD's products are solid rather than unique; it is strong in direct investing (TD Direct Investing), cards (TD Aeroplan) and insurance, but there is no independent evidence that its core banking products are best in class.

marketShare.market: Revenue of Canada's Big Five banks (RBC, TD, BMO, Scotiabank, CIBC)
marketShare.measure: share of combined reported FY2025 total revenue (C$237,530M), calculated from each bank's FY2025 earnings release

threats: The US asset cap (US$434 billion of combined US bank assets) and ongoing AML consent orders limit growth in US Banking; TD expects about US$550M of remediation spend in FY2026 and its Suspicious Activity Report lookback to run into calendar 2027.
FINTRAC's ongoing review of TD's enterprise AML remediation in Canada may lead to further regulatory action.
A Canadian housing downturn or tariff-driven recession hitting its large mortgage, card and commercial loan books (PCL was C$4,506M in FY2025).
Falling interest rates and deposit competition squeezing net interest margins.
Digital challengers (Wealthsimple, EQ Bank, Tangerine) and open banking eroding fee income and deposit share among younger Canadians.
Execution risk in its restructuring and C$2-2.5B cost-savings program, and in the wind-down of US retail cards and point-of-sale financing.

ceo.name: Raymond Chun
ceo.background: Joined TD in 1992 as a management associate; former COO, Group Head of Canadian Personal Banking and CEO of TD Insurance; BA from the University of Western Ontario and MBA from Queen's University

c1.evidence: TD is a leader in Canadian banking, a mature, slow-growing industry, not an emerging one.

c2.evidence: Clients choose TD for convenience, its branch network and its full product range (TD Aeroplan cards, TD Direct Investing, TD Insurance), and Canada's five-bank oligopoly makes that durable, but the products are similar to rivals' and its US reputation was damaged by the 2024 AML guilty plea.

c3.evidence: Almost every Canadian and many East Coast Americans know the green TD brand and it is one of Canada's two default big banks, but RBC ranked highest among the Big Five in J.D. Power's 2025 Canadian satisfaction study and few customers enthuse about a bank.

c4.evidence: TD's purpose 'to enrich the lives of our customers, communities and colleagues' is backed by its TD Ready Commitment community program, but management under CEO Raymond Chun is focused mainly on ROE targets (16% by FY2029) and AML remediation.

c6.evidence: “big, convenient, Canadian, money-laundering scandal”: people see TD as one of Canada's largest and most convenient banks, an impression that is mostly positive in Canada but tarnished by the 2024 US anti-money-laundering guilty plea and US$3.088B in penalties.

c7.evidence: Banking, wealth and insurance are huge markets growing with the economy and savings, but they are not riding a fast secular trend like AI or cloud.

c8.evidence: TD can grow fee businesses such as wealth, TD Cowen and insurance, but its US bank is constrained by the US$434B asset cap and its name and model tie it to banking.

m1.evidence: Chun set out a clear plan at the September 29, 2025 Investor Day ('Deeper, Faster, Disciplined', targeting 16% ROE and 7-10% EPS growth by FY2029 and scaling AI), but it is a turnaround plan rather than a bold vision of the future.

m2.evidence: Chun has spent his whole career at TD since 1992 and is managing for the long term, but he is a professional steward who became CEO only in February 2025, not a founder.

m4.evidence: Chun came up through customer-facing businesses (TD Insurance, TD Direct Investing, Canadian Personal Banking) and stresses deepening client relationships, but there is no strong public evidence of exceptional servant leadership.

m5.evidence: TD's culture is that of a large conservative bank now prioritising risk and controls and AML remediation over inventing new products.

m6.evidence: Chun has a BA from Western and an MBA from Queen's and a background in banking and insurance management, not engineering.

m7.evidence: Chun has no known personal integrity issues and has made AML remediation TD's top priority, but he was a senior executive during the years when TD's US AML failures occurred.

m7b.evidence: No record found of Raymond Chun giving a commencement speech at Stanford, Harvard, MIT or a similar top university.

m8b.evidence: Chun has a low-key, measured banker's public persona rather than a distinctive celebrity personality.

m9.evidence: Since February 2025 Chun sold the Schwab stake (C$8,975M pre-tax gain), restructured the US balance sheet and lifted Q3 2026 reported net income to C$4,615M from C$3,336M a year earlier with a 15.8% ROE, but his tenure is short.

m10.evidence: TD is not known for frugality, though it is now cutting costs with a C$2-2.5B annualized savings target and fewer management layers.

c10.evidence: TD keeps savings safe and funds homes and businesses for over 27 million clients in Canada and the US, important but not life-changing on a global scale.

p2.evidence: Running a C$2.1 trillion bank safely is hard and important to the Canadian economy, but many large banks provide the same services.

f1.evidence: Reported revenue rose from C$43,646M in FY2020 to C$67,777M in FY2025 with one dip in FY2021 (C$42,693M), though FY2025 includes the C$8,975M Schwab gain and nine-month FY2026 revenue (C$49,267M) is below the prior-year C$52,283M.

f2.evidence: Net margin went from 27.3% in FY2020 to 30.3% in FY2025 but swung widely (15.5% in FY2024 after AML penalties); gross margin is not meaningful for a bank.

f3.evidence: As a bank TD is heavily leveraged (total liabilities C$1,984,846M vs equity C$127,015M at July 31, 2026), but its CET1 ratio of 14.3% is well above regulatory minimums and equity is positive.

f4.evidence: Reported net income rose from C$11,895M in FY2020 to C$20,538M in FY2025 but fell to C$8,842M in FY2024; bank operating cash flow swings with deposits and trading and is not a useful trend.

v1.evidence: TD is a strong all-round bank, but there is no single practical reason an ordinary person would pick it over RBC or the other big banks, whose products are similar.

v2.evidence: With more than 100,000 colleagues TD is a well-known Canadian employer and graduate recruiter, but it does not top global best-workplace rankings and is currently cutting non-client-facing roles.

c5.evidence: If TD vanished, millions of Canadians and East Coast Americans would lose their bank, mortgage lender and insurer and markets would be disrupted, but other big banks could absorb its customers over time.
